<h1>Slew and CC smoothing</h1>

CC slew interpolates outgoing controller values between successive arp steps
so a moving filter cutoff or resonance glides instead of stepping. The
**slew view** offers three modes: off, eight manual glide times, and an auto
mode that stretches the glide to reach the next CC target, so sparse arps
glide longer and dense arps snap tighter.

A second, smaller smoother sits on LaunchControl fader and knob input before it
reaches a sequencer parameter. It is not user-configurable.

---

## Slew view

### LP layout

While the slew view is active, both Launchpads display the same 8×8
picture:

- **LHS LP** (both players): sequencers 1–8, one column per sequencer.
  Only the sequencers that carry CC arps have a slew column: **2, 3 and
  6**. Columns 1, 4, 5, 7 and 8 stay dark.
- **RHS LP** (both players): sequencers 9–16, and again only the
  CC-carrying ones: **9, 11 and 12**, which are RHS columns 1, 3 and 4.
  Column 2 (sequencer 10) and columns 5–8 (sequencers 13–16) stay dark.

A column is live for sequencers 2, 3, 6, 9, 11 and 12, the same set that owns a
CC-arp view. There is nothing for slew to smooth on the others, so they
render dark and ignore presses.

Each live column represents one sequencer. The column shows one of three
modes:

- **Off**: row 1 slate grey, rows 2–8 dark.
- **Manual level N**: rows 1 to N lit in that sequencer's own colour, the rest
  dark, so the column reads as a bar whose height is the glide time.
- **Auto mode**: row 1 in the sequencer's own colour, row 8 purple, the rows
  between dark. Auto follows the trig pattern (see *Behaviour* below).

### Edit gestures

Slew is edited by **pressing a column/row cell on either LP**. Both players
can edit and the surface is shared, but each player's modifiers are their own,
so a shift+mute on one LC does not affect the other.

| Current tau | Press | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Row 1 | tau = 1 (turn on at level 1) |
| 1 | Row 1 | tau = 0 (turn off) |
| 2..9 | Row 1 | tau = 1 (change to level 1; exits auto) |
| N | Row N (2..7) | no-op (idempotent) |
| Other than N | Row N (2..7) | tau = N |
| 0 | Row 8 | tau = 8 (turn on at level 8) |
| 8 | Row 8 | tau = 9 (enter auto) |
| 9 | Row 8 | tau = 8 (exit auto → manual 8) |
| 1..7 | Row 8 | tau = 8 |
| any | SHIFT + MUTE (player's own LC), any row | tau = 0 (column reset) |
| any | Any column outside `{2, 3, 6, 9, 11, 12}` | ignored |

There is no single "off" cell that always disables slew. To turn off
without shift-mute: press row 1 once (lands at tau=1), then press row 1
again (tau=0). SHIFT + MUTE is the one-press panic reset.

### Behaviour

**Off** sends each CC value the moment the step fires, so the parameter jumps.

**Manual levels 1 to 8** glide over a fixed time, from about 20 ms at level 1
to about two seconds at level 8, doubling roughly every level. The whole
sequencer uses the same time, so every CC row on it moves together.

**Auto** sets the glide from the pattern instead. Each row looks ahead to its
own next CC target and takes exactly that long to get there, so a row with a
target every step snaps, and a row with one target per bar glides across the
whole bar. Rows on the same sequencer can end up sounding quite different, and
that is the point: a busy filter-cutoff row and a sparse delay-time row each
get the glide that suits them. Because the glide is measured in steps, it
follows the tempo and the sequencer's clock division.

A changed glide time takes effect on that row's next step rather than
immediately, which is not something you will hear at any sensible tempo.
A glide already in progress finishes with the setting it started on.

## LC 1-pole filter

This one is not a view at all. It is a smoother that sits on every
LaunchControl knob, all three rows of them, taking the jitter out of the
knob's own output so a slow turn does not produce a staircase. The knob's
0-127 travel is quantised to the eight values the rest of the instrument
works in, and a fast sweep arrives as one clean transition per value rather
than a burst.

There is no LP gesture for this filter. It exists so that sweeping a knob
across several values in one motion sends the engine one clean transition
per value rather than a burst of intermediate ones.
